subtype: Approach: critical path thinking about dependent tasks [Thinking]
passage: I'm Imran, on the web team. In the second week I noticed Kiran at the whiteboard with a tangle of arrows between tasks. The mobile screens depended on the API. So did our web pages. Kiran drew the longest chain in red: API contract, then mobile and web side by side, then integration, then release. "If the contract slips, everything behind it slips," Kiran said, and booked a two-hour session with both teams that week. We argued over field names, dates and error messages, and by Friday the contract was written down and shared. Mobile and web started work on the same Monday. I can't tell whether Kiran had done this before. It only looked obvious afterwards.

qa.q: What did Kiran book with both teams that week?
qa.a: Kiran booked a two-hour session with both teams.

qa.q: What was Kiran probably worried about when drawing the red chain?
qa.a: Kiran was probably worried that a slipped contract would hold up everything behind it.

qa.q: What else could Kiran do to protect the plan, and why?
qa.a: Kiran could make sure nobody changes the contract without telling both teams, because a quiet change could break the work already started.

qa.q: How might the mobile team have seen the early session?
qa.a: The mobile team probably felt relieved that their work would not be stuck waiting, since the contract was settled before either team began building.

grounding: Illustrates a lead seeing that one contract blocks two teams and settling it early with both, so the longest chain of dependent tasks is not delayed.
